headline: The Fair Next Week.
article:
The Twentieth annual exhibition of the Litch. field County Agricultural Society, commences on Wednesday of next week, and holds two days.

 We need only call attention of those interes ted to the date, and we are sure that the farmers manufacturers and stock-growers of the county will do the rest,to make this the most successful fair ever held in Litchfeld.

 Last year the very unfavorahle weather seri- ously interfered with the pecuniary success of the exhibition, and the committee have thus changed the time of holding the fair, to the first week in October, to avoid, if possible, the chan ces of poor day, and at any rate to be after the equinoctial storm rather than to have it afte, them.

 Already larger number of animals of the cat tie kind have been promised for the exhibition than usual, and the society hope to secure a large attendance of fine stock horses to add to the interest of the occasion.

 The Committee, however, have done well to offer the greater proportion of their premiums for the best stock other than horses although these have not been disregarded,-an for the produce of the farm, the loom and the workshop, rather than for fast time on the track.

 Their Society is an agricultural one, simply and they advertise Cattle Show and Fair, and not horse fair, or an exhibition for horse. yacing. Farmers and others will note this, and be more ready to bring their stock and their wares to Fair where they will be properly no ticed and rewarded, according to their merit in their various classes. There will be horses too, and fine enough, and fast enough, without going out of the States to find them.

 The address of Gov. Holley on Thursday, is looked forward too with fattering anticipations, which will we doubt not be abundantly fulfilled.

 The Plymouth Brass Band have been secured to enliven the Fair with their excellent music and concert of Ltchfeld County singers-one of the kind of years gone by-is announced which will give great additional attraction te the occasion.

 It is desired particularly by the committee that there should be large display of Fruit al the Fair, in recognition of the abundance of tht season, and certainly nothing will so largely con tribute to the interest and elegance of the exhi bition, than @ successful display in this depart ment.

 Altogether the exhibition promises to be thu most interesting and rewarding Fair thatthe Agri cultural Society has held in years, and we advise all of our readers in the county, who have an in terest in contributing to and visiting an old-timt Cattle Show, and who have the honor and wei fare and prosperity of the county at heart, tt come up hither, bri: ging their sheaOes with them and their wives and children, their stock ant produce, and the stranger that is within thei gates!

Suppose the battle between Lee and Gram


Is indecisive, or suppose the .enemy gan
such advantages as to compel Lee TO fai


back toward Richmond, are we at all pre-


pared for such contingency Candol
compels a negative answer. for we have
been so elated by success after success tha


we have not permitted ourselves to contem'
plate the probability of anything but vic
tory. This is not wise. The reaction from
the elated condition in which we have beer
for months past may carry us to the other
extreme, and at a time when the highest
qualities of manhood may be needed to re-
pair n temporary reverse we will be found
in state of supine dependency. We should
at once look OH the other side of the picture
and accustom ourselves to the idea OF
temporary miscarriage of our arms, and to
the requirements of such an event. While
the auspices were never more favorable fol-
Lee, the chances of battle are so various
and so much beyond human control that ii
is impossible to foretell with certainty the
issue of the pending engagement. A year
ago "Stonewall' Jackson fell not far from
the spot on which Lee and Grant are about
to join battle. What If Lee should fall!
May Providence spare us this calamity, for
the people of the Confederacy are by no
means prepared for it.


We all know this, yet no one has asked
the question: What are we to do if Lee
suffers reverse, and is forced to Tall back
upon this city? Still less have we permit
ted ourselves to consider the consequences
of deplorable accident which may hap
pen any day. They have made up their
minds, unwisely, that the war must end
one way or the other this year, forgetting,
quite that there can be but one way. If
Lee should fall and his army be unsuccess-
full, we greatly fear that the majority of the
people would begin to look the other way.

verse of his army, nor the two together,
will justify the contemplation of that other
way. Let it be dismissed at once and for
ever. Suppose Lee falls, we have Beaure-
gard. Suppose his army fails to drive off
Grant and has to retire, we have reinforce
ments and many excellent lines of de-
fense. Whatever betides, this is very
clear. Our independence must be won.-

no middle ground, as Mr.. Leach fancies, be-
tween independence and subjugation. How
often have we proclaimed that the fall of
Richmond, and of all our cities, would not,
and should not, end the war. Do we still
stand fast to that proclamation, or are we,
indeed, ready to see the war end this year,
one way or the other. Perhaps at this mo-
ment the great contest on the Rapidan is at
its height, and before the setting of this
days sun, the wires may bring us sad
tidings. Should it so chance we must set
hard the teeth and rally once more to the
breach remembering that the cause for
which Stonewall" jackson died may suf-
fer thousand reverses, but can never fail
The mishaps of to-day may be repaired to-
morrow, and in the end we will, for we
must, triumph gloriously.

headline: SLAVES OF DEBT.
article:
In would be curious speculation
to inquire how long the people OF Eu-
rope will be likely to endure the enor-
nous load of debt under which they
are now grooming. No one believes
that the principal of the European
debts can be paid, and the war goes
on year by year, adding to both prln-
cipal and interest. If these frequent
" returning wars do not soon come to
an end it will be impossible to pay ev-
en- the interest Of these debts. Then
the great powers of the world will be
reduced to the condition of Turkey,
and be compelled to repudiate, and il
they 90 to war at all, carry it on in a
crippled and inefficient way. The on
lv use of their intOlerable debts that
any one can see is to compel the ma
tons, finally, to keep the peace.


At present, however, the people OF
Europe are slaves of debt. All the
fruits of their toll go to pay the inter
est on the enormous national Obllga-
tions. A condition of debt like this
is oppressive to all true freedom and
manliness. There is no form Of slav
cry more oppressive to nations or in
dividuals than that of debt.


The American people should take
timely warning from European exam

exists here should be paid off as soor

headline: RUSSIAN INFLUENZA.
article:
timely Article From the Medical News


soI Phiiadelphia-How to Apprehend,


Avoid and Treat the Malady which is


Becoming Epidemic Throughout the


Country.


PHILADELPHIA. Dec. 29.-The Medical
News of this city publishes an article
on influenza - ia grippe" - by Prof.
Robsrs bartholomew, of Jefferson Med
ical college. After giving an historical
sketch of the disease, its pathology
and morbid anatomy, the author says:


Influenza comes suddenly; goes as quick
ly. The least robust, at any age, and women
seem to be the first victims. 1t is here a
question of bodily condition, not of the sex.
The large numbers simultaneously attacked
attracts general attention, and those most
impressionable are seized, the onset being
facilitated by any depressing emotion like
fear or illness. There is no rigor, properly,
to be thus designated, but rather a series OF
light chlls and feeling of heat Herewith.
Sometimes malaise of a general kind is ex-
perienced, but, like the attack itself, it is
short in duration, lasting but few hours.


With the first access of the nasal and fau-
cial irritation comes the chilliness, which is
followed by some feverishness, with more
pronounced malaise and, in general, the
headache, weakness and soreness of the
me mbers, especially of the larger joints.
With the progress of the case in some epi-
denies there is considerable weakness, even
marked depressions of the vital powers. The
pulse becomes small and weak, the mind
gloomy and restlessness ensues. When a
fatal termination is to occur, as rule, an
extension downward into the trachea and
brOnch takes place.


Although catarrhal and croupous pneu-
monia are said to be complications" they
should be regarded as occasional conditions,
ana when present are, properly speaking,
constituted parts of the malady. The chief
Importance of croupous and catarrhal pneu-
mona is that the development of these, out
of an existing catarrh of the bronchi, is fire.
quently cause of death.


The rapdity with which the disease super
venes-its preliminary development being
hours, and its whole duration but matter
of three or four days-is remarkable Re
lapseS are common, usually each sue
ceeding seizure being milder, but not few
pass by easy transition into chronic bron-
chits, emphysema, asthma, etc.


Obviously a catarrhal process, extensive
and severe, may contribute immensely to
chronic disease of the middle ear, eustachian
tube, nose and throat, and thus permanently
damage the parts.


The best manner of securing immunity is
by the inhalation of suphurous acid gas
daily, when the approach of the epidemic
renders it necessary, and by taking five
grains of salicylate of cinchonidine three
times day and by so living as to avoid tax
ing cold.


When the attack has begun it seems to
me desirable to give or grains of calomel
at night, inhale some sulphurous acid gas
and have tie patient sit in a room whore
steamcontaining eucalyptol can be inhaled
in large quantities. The Insulation of res
orcin, and dusting over the entire area of the
affected parts as far as practicable, is also
recommended. The internal remedy most
desirable is atropine in solution-1 grain to
ounce. of water-dose being from l to 5
drops, the minimum being for little children
(after first dentition). The tincture of bella :
donna may be used, from one to ten drops
twice a day. As this medicament is both
prompt and prolonged in action, it should
be given not more than twice a day, unless
the dose be much smaller than is advised
above.


Salicylate of cinchonidne and quinine
should be given as prophylactic remedy,
if there be reason to suppose that such
power is really exerted by it.


My own conviction is that as prophy
Tactic the combination of cinchonidine with
salcylic acid is preferable to quinne. For
the depression and melancholy it is proba-
BILE that atropine will do better. For the
distressing headache, joint pains and wake
fulness, antipyrin, acetanild, phenacetin
and other germcdes and antiseptics will,
no doubt, be found useful.

headline: NOTORIOUS WOMAN ARRESTED
article:
NOTORIOUS WOMAN ARRESTED
profound sensation was caused in
Winchester yesterday afternoon by the
arrest of Susan Barber, notorious col
ored woman, OH a charge of manslaugh;er
and infanticide, in having caused the
death of Mrs. Margaret Athey, the
pretty young wife of Oscar Athey, by an
illegal operation. The Barber woman's
arrest was the outcome of deathbed
confession made by Mrs. Athey to her
physician. The Barber woman per-
formed the illegal operation upon the dy-
ing Mrs. Athey at her own request. The
dying woman also said that her husband
had repeatedly begged her not to undergo
the operation, and with her very last
breath she exonerated him from all
blame. Margaret Barber was committed
to Jail without bail for hearing. For
many years she has been a notorious
character, and many CHASTITY stories of
crime concerning her have from time to
time been told. The finding of the dead
bodies of infants buried near the spots
where she has lived were attributed to
her, but no direct evidence has ever been
forthcoming, and in consequence she has
escaped punishment. The woman is
nearly 70 years of age, and although she
is colored person, her skin is white and
parchment like.

headline: Domestic Science In The Schools
article:
The education that does not recognize
sex difference is rapidly passing away,
The most hopeful note in modern pro-
gress is that educators, sociologists and
philanthropist have come to realize the
necessity of an educational system that
developes women for the home, that
recognizes those peculiar problems of
physique and function which mark the
necessary divergence of educational
methods between the sexes.


An initial phase Of this movement is
the introduction of domestic science in
to many Of the private and public
schools of the country, and 1t is only a
question of time when no school sys-
tenn will deny to its pupils such train
ing. The servant problem the pure
food problem, the race suicide problem
and many Others sociological difficulties
will be solved largely by this system
that educates girls as girls.

article:
Although it is of course unknown whether the report that w. c. Davis of Jasper will enter the congressional fight in the Sixth district against Capt. Rich mond P. Hobson is true or not, it is known that Captain Hobson is already preparing against any political thunder which his defense of the Brownsville sol diers might furnish a prospective oppo- nent.

 Edgar L. Clarkson, private secretary of Captain Hobson, has sent out the fol- lowing statement as coming from the con- gressman. in which statement Mir. Hobson defends his action;

 ''The action of the President prevented a proper investigation of the crime com mtted by the negro soldiers. There is reason to believe a regular court of in- quiry and then courtmartial would have found out the guilty, and hanged them on the spot, which should have been done, and the innocent exonerated. headline: TEMPERANCE COMING
article:
In her stirring address before the
National w. c. I. U. convention at
Asbury Park, N. j., and later speaking
before the house judiciary committee
In Washington, Mrs. Mary Harris Ar
NOR. the Georgia cyclone" gave some
OF the reasons why we may look for


saloonless nation in 1920" We
| quote:


I believe that Jesus Christ meant
what he said and said what he meant
when he declared. All power Is given
unto me In heaven and In earth and |
believe that the God who made the
sun stand still on Gideon, and the
moon on Ajalon, at the cry of his
nghting. praying, believing servant,
Joshua, is perfectly able to smash the
liquor traffic into everlasting smither-
Gems, whenever we get ready.


The old order changes, giving
place to new. and God fulfllls himself
In many ways He has promised the
destruction Of the liquor traffic in these
words, Every tree that bringeth not
forth good fruit Is hewn down and
cast into the fire. Certainly no man
would say that the liquor traffic brings
forth good fruit; hence the liquor
traffic must go.


One OF the ways in which God Is
fulfilling this promise is through his
eternal truth in science. King Alco-
hol has marched down the ages for
these thousands Of years, conquering
and to conquer, until the centuries
sob with a ceaseless SORROW but at
last science has burst the blood-rust-
ed chain that bound her for a thou
sand years, has seized the shining two
edged sword OF Gods eternal truth,
and challenges the monster to mortal
combat. To doubt the issue Is to doubt
the sanity Of the human race and the
power of the everlasting God.


Il believe we shall have a saloonless
nation in 1920, because public senti-
ment is opposed to the liquor traffic.
The persistent education along scien-
tho temperance lines, instituted by
the Woman's Christian Temperance
union years ago, is bearing fruit today
in mighty army Of young men and
young women in the various religious
and philanthropic organizations In
our schools and colleges. and even In
the halls OF congress.


The liquor traffic is doomed to
speedy destruction because 1t Is op-
posed to common sense. Hasn't 1t al
ways been opposed to common sense?
Yes. but people have not been exer-
cising their common sense In this d.
rection until comparatively recent
years. for two reasons: First. be-
cause Gods eternal truth in science
had not been revealed on this cues
ton as 1t is today; second, the world
is better today than ever before, and
the public mind Is obsessed with the
idea OF the preservation and prolonga-
ton OF human life. Eugenics is the
most popular fad of the day. City,
state, and national governments are
looking after the health OF the people
as never before. They swat the ny,
they go on a still hunt for the mos
quito, they beard the hookworm In his
den, and the germs must fly for their
lives The human race has learned
that no man liveth to himself and no
man dieth to himself and reforma-
ton Is the watchword of the hour;
hence men are training their common
sense on this question, and the liquor
traffic must go

81 think-come in, cOmrade. / will

For the name of Haeckel was, just
then, one curiously significant.


He disappeared, and old Adelbert
waited When the doorkeeper re-
turned, it was to tell him to follow
him, and to lead the way downstairs.


Two or three students came toward
him at once. ''You are seeking
Haeckel?" one of them asked.
"I am. I knew him, but not well.

herew


The students exchanged glances.
'eHe is not here,' one said. "Where
did you know him?"


''He came frequently to shop /

hood meeting place. A fine lad. I
liked him. But recently he has not
come, and knowing his corps, came
here to find him."


They had hoped to learn something
from him, and he knew nothing. He
has disappeared" they told him. 'He
is not at his lodging, and he has left
his classes. He went away suddenly,
leaving everything. That is all we
know"


1t sounded sinister. Old Adelbert,
heavy hearted, turned away and
climbed again to the street. That gate
way was closed, too. And he felt a
pang of uneasiness. What could have
happened to the boy? Was the world,
after all, only a place Of trouble?


But now came good fortune, and,
like evil, it came not singly. The
operation was over, and his daughter
on the mend. The fee was paid also.
And the second followed on the heels
Of the first.


He did not like Americans. Too
often, in better days, had he heard the
merits of the American republic COM
pared with the shortcomings of his
own government. When, as happened
now and then, he met the American
family on the staircase, he drew
sharply aside that no touch of repub-
licanism might contaminate his uni
form.


On that day, however, things
changed.


First of all, he met the American
lad in the hallway, and was pleased
to see him doff his bit Of cap. Not
many, nowadays, uncovered head to
him. The American lad was going
down; Adelbert was climbing, one step

of provisions.


The American boy, having passed,
turned, hesitated, went back. I'D

81 am very strong" said the Ameri-

So Adelbert gave up his basket, and
the two went, up. Four long flights
of stone stairs led to Adelbert's room.
The ascent took time and patience.


At the door Adelbert paused. Then,
loneliness overcoming prejudice,
"Come in" he said.


The bare little room appealed to the
boy. 'It's very nice, isn't it?" he
said. There's nothing to fall over"

He ranged the room, frankly curious,

who lived in box tied to the window
sill, and asked for crumbs for them.
Adelbert brought bread from his small
store.


The boy cheered him. His interest
in the old saber, the intentness with
which he listened to it's history, the
politeness with which he ignored his
hosts inirmity, all won the old mans
heart.

headline:
Captain Monckton, in Tanning New Guinea,
Writes a Moving Picture Record of


Dangerous Days
article:
voted to the navigation Of curious
things that contrive to keep on top Of
the water, with here and there pas
sages Of real ocean stuff, big waves
and the howl of the wind. And one
cannot overlook those other pages that
give pictures of the dangers of diving
Tor pearls, the nature of good pearl
grounds and the habits of peculiar and
deadly fish. Monckton met Captain
Siocum while on visit to Sydney and
admired that old New Bedford salts
pluck in circumnavigating the globe in
his yawl Spray.


But we are getting beyond our depth
or limit in this review. The powers
that be in New Guinea soon saw what
Monckton had in him and made him
resident magistrate. We don't believe
iE extended quotations from book in
any notice in these columns, but no
better idea of what this man was up
against can be obtained than that pre-
sented in his own statement Of orders
and advice given to him on The day of
his commission:


"Now, then, here is list Of things
that need attending at once. There Is
murder at Awaiama, a man cut his
mother-in-law's throat, catch him; there
is to be new mission station at Cape
Vogel, survey and buy the land for the
natives; Fellows is in trouble at the
Nd ~,<.
Bromilow has collected a lot of orphans
at Dobu, go and mandate them to the
mission; man named Ryan has shot
native at Ferguson Island, arrest him
and inquire into the case; Carruth has
been supplying grog to the natives on
Burns, catch Carruth and deal with him;
the Siai's decks need caulking and she
needs new wire rigging; I've got the
wire, but there is no money with which
to pay any one to do the job Patten
has got into some sort Of trouble at the
south end of Goodenough, find out what
it's all about; Thompson has started a
cocoanut plantation on the northeast
coast Of the island, look him up and see
that he is all right; when you get some
spare time, go and buy cargo of vans
for the Jail, and don't pay more than
los per ton for them; see that Billy, the
cook, shuts the pub at IL o'clock, there
are only fights and rows if he is open
later. Don't use the police for arresting
white men il you can possibly avoid;
arrest them yourself"


There's program that calls on the
pluck and mental resources of a real
man. If you are looking for book that
mingles cool intrepidity with canny eau
ton, one always giving native back
ground of rich hues, get a copy of
Tanning New Guinea and read it.
